items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 248: Minutes of directors' meetings
items.quote: The records must be kept for at least ten years from the date of the meeting.
items.why: The binding rule and the source of the figure. Every company must cause minutes of all proceedings at directors' meetings to be recorded and kept for at least ten years; failure is an offence by every officer in default, punishable by a fine. The section does not say what a minute must contain.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 249: Minutes as evidence
items.quote: are evidence (in Scotland, sufficient evidence) of the proceedings at the meeting
items.why: Why the minute book matters in a dispute. Minutes authenticated by the chair of the meeting or of the next meeting are evidence of the proceedings, and until the contrary is proved the meeting is deemed duly held and its proceedings duly to have taken place.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 172: Duty to promote the success of the company
items.why: The duty the criterion's top level refers to. A director must act in the way he or she considers, in good faith, most likely to promote the company's success, having regard to long-term consequences, employees, suppliers and customers, the community and environment, and reputation. The section does not mention records or minutes, and no safe harbour appears in it.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 414CZA: Section 172(1) statement
items.quote: describes how the directors have had regard to the matters set out in section 172(1)(a) to (f)
items.why: The one statutory duty to report on how the section 172 matters were considered. The strategic report must include the statement; it does not apply to a company that qualifies as medium-sized. A board cannot write it honestly without records of what was considered.

items.title: Companies Act 2006, section 1157: Power of court to grant relief in certain cases
items.quote: he acted honestly and reasonably, and that having regard to all the circumstances of the case
items.why: The nearest thing in statute to protection for a careful director, and it is discretionary: where an officer is or may be liable for negligence, default, breach of duty or breach of trust but acted honestly and reasonably and ought fairly to be excused, the court may relieve him wholly or in part. Records are how reasonableness is shown; the section does not say so.

items.title: Practice Direction 57AD: Disclosure in the Business and Property Courts
items.locator: Paras 2.2, 2.5-2.6 (meaning of document), 3.1 (disclosure duties), 4.1-4.5 (preservation), 13.1 (native format, metadata)
items.quote: It also extends to metadata, and other embedded data which is not typically visible on screen or a printout.
items.why: Source of the brief's quotation. In the Business and Property Courts of England and Wales, a person who knows it is or may become a party to proceedings must take reasonable steps to preserve relevant documents, including those a retention policy would otherwise delete, and must disclose known adverse documents. Documents include deleted information and metadata, so a record's creation date is itself evidence. Page shows 'Updated: Thursday, 29 September 2022'. Practice Direction 31B, read alongside, applies similar preservation duties elsewhere.

items.title: Algorithmic Transparency Recording Standard: guidance for public sector bodies
items.locator: Section 2 ('ATRS purpose and scope'); sections 5-13 (the template tiers)
items.quote: Enable senior responsible owners to take meaningful accountability for algorithmic tools and their outputs
items.why: A ready-made structure for a per-system record: owner and responsibility, description and rationale, deployment context, tool and model specification, data, risks, mitigations and impact assessments. Mandatory by policy, not statute, for government departments and for arm's length bodies delivering public services, for tools with a significant influence on decisions with public effect. Updated 8 May 2025.

items.title: Artificial Intelligence Risk Management Framework (AI RMF 1.0), NIST AI 100-1
items.publisher: National Institute of Standards and Technology
items.locator: Section 5.1 (GOVERN), document page 22 (page 27 of the PDF); MAP 2.2; MEASURE 3.1
items.quote: Documentation can enhance transparency, improve human review processes, and bolster accountability in AI system teams.
items.why: International comparator. A voluntary United States framework that treats documentation as part of governance, not an afterthought: roles, system limits, test results and risk tracking are each to be documented. Also says processes for independent review can reduce internal bias.

items.title: Code of Practice for the Cyber Security of AI
items.publisher: Department for Science, Innovation and Technology
items.locator: Principle 8 ('Document your data, models and prompts'), provisions 8.1 and 8.1.1
items.quote: Developers shall document and maintain a clear audit trail of their system design and post-deployment maintenance plans.
items.why: A voluntary government code. Developers keep an audit trail of design and maintenance plans and pass documentation down to operators, covering sources of training data, intended scope and limitations, guardrails, retention time and failure modes. Tells a buyer what record to ask a supplier for.

items.title: AI Act, Article 26: Obligations of deployers of high-risk AI systems (AI Act Service Desk copy)
items.locator: Article 26(5)-(6); 'About this text' notice. Article 73 (serious incident reporting) read alongside
items.quote: Deployers of high-risk AI systems shall keep the logs automatically generated by that high-risk AI system to the extent such logs are under their control
items.why: The Commission's own copy, not the Official Journal (EUR-Lex returned an empty page); it says the text follows the EUR-Lex consolidated version as at 27 July 2026. Deployers of high-risk systems must keep automatically generated logs under their control for at least six months. On the Commission's copy of Article 113 these high-risk duties apply from 2 December 2027 for Annex III systems. Relevant only to organisations within the Act's reach.
